The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "An Illustrated Guide to Masked Wrestlers": https://pudding.cool/2020/05/wrestling/
The files: data/wrestlers.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by looking at the data folder and reading the story.

Terms Termes
- Babyface (face): A wrestler who is heroic and follows the rules. Fans usually cheer him on.
- Booking: Determination of the way the match progresses, as well as the events to follow. Similar to a script in cinema.
- Botch: Poorly executed booking or hold.
- Bump: A fall on the ground or in the ring. It is the first thing that a wrestler has to master.
- Feud: Rivalry between wrestlers, usually spread out over several matches.
- Gimmick: Role embodied by a wrestler in the ring.
- Heat: Shouts from the crowd for a wrestler. The more a heel recieves, the better he is.
- Heel (rudo): A wrestler with a violent or cheating gimmick. The babyface's adversary, their goal is to be booed by the public.
- Job: Unrewarding but essential work in wrestling which consisters of losing to another wrestler, in order to highlight the other's talent.
- Kayfabe: The illusion maintained around wrestling to make everything seem real. The term comes from "carny", slang used by fairground people, by inversing the word "fake" ("kay-fay"=>kayfabe)
- Mark: A person who believes, or lets himself believe, that wrestling is real. The term was used in the fairground to designate gullible people, who were "marked" (with a chalk sign for example) without them knowing.
- Pop: Positive reaction from the crowd, usually after a spectacular hold or the victory of a beloved wrestler. The more a babyface receives, the better he is.
- Push: Putting a wrestler forward, following a decision by the bookers or a growing popularity with the public.
- Screwjob: The final result of a match deemed unfair by the public. It can be scripted or not, as in the case of the Montreal Screwjob, between Shawn Michaels and Bret Hart, where the latter lost the belt without being warned.
- Shoot: Action which breaks the kayfabe (ex: calling a wrestler by their real name). It can be scripted or not.
- Smart: Designates a wrestling enthusiast who knows the behind the scenes of wrestling or is looking to learn more.
- Spot: Action or series of actions constituting highlights of a match. Generally generates a strong public reaction. However, too many spots can damage the psychology of the match and saturate the public. Wrestlers are then pejoratively described as "spot monkeys".
- Squash: A wrestler's expeditive victory. The squash is often used to put a monster heel in the spotlight.
- Stiff: Execution of holds with excessive force. This allows the wrestler to intensify the match but with the risk of injuring their opponent.
- Turn: When a wrestler changes their alignment, going from heel to face, or vice versa. The turn generally provokes a strong public reaction.
- Tweener: A wrestler that cannot be easily classified as a face or a heel. His gimmick is often that of a rebel or an antihero who opposes authority. He can therefore break the rules while still being supported by the public.
My name is Gwen, and I am a French journalist and graphic designer, and have been a fan of wrestling since I was 10 years old.
For me, the mask is the best symbol in wrestling. It is immediately recognizable and unique for every wrestler. I started out drawing them just for fun at first, but through my research I discovered passionate lives that I wanted to share.
For this publication, we have limited ourselves to around 200 wrestlers (though more will be added) chosen according to their importance in wrestling or for their specific interests. Details were primarily derived from sources available on the Internet (Wikipedia, press articles, and fansites), and also the sites Luchawiki, Cagematch, and Wrestling database. Additional information comes from Heather Levi’s book “The World of Lucha Libre”.
Although I am a wrestling fan, I do not claim to be an expert. This subject is complicated for a journalist because reality and fiction are permanently intertwined in order to maintain the illusion (or kayfabe) of the storylines. We are always open to any suggestions or for improvement or correction.
Whether you are a fan, or maybe even a wrestler, please don’t hesitate to contact us to enrich this database. I would be particularly interested in a masked wrestler’s experiences, in order to know more about their connection to their mask. Get in touch at sup@pudding.cool.

Terms Termes
- Babyface (face): A wrestler who is heroic and follows the rules. Fans usually cheer him on.
- Booking: Determination of the way the match progresses, as well as the events to follow. Similar to a script in cinema.
- Botch: Poorly executed booking or hold.
- Bump: A fall on the ground or in the ring. It is the first thing that a wrestler has to master.
- Feud: Rivalry between wrestlers, usually spread out over several matches.
- Gimmick: Role embodied by a wrestler in the ring.
- Heat: Shouts from the crowd for a wrestler. The more a heel recieves, the better he is.
- Heel (rudo): A wrestler with a violent or cheating gimmick. The babyface's adversary, their goal is to be booed by the public.
- Job: Unrewarding but essential work in wrestling which consisters of losing to another wrestler, in order to highlight the other's talent.
- Kayfabe: The illusion maintained around wrestling to make everything seem real. The term comes from "carny", slang used by fairground people, by inversing the word "fake" ("kay-fay"=>kayfabe)
- Mark: A person who believes, or lets himself believe, that wrestling is real. The term was used in the fairground to designate gullible people, who were "marked" (with a chalk sign for example) without them knowing.
- Pop: Positive reaction from the crowd, usually after a spectacular hold or the victory of a beloved wrestler. The more a babyface receives, the better he is.
- Push: Putting a wrestler forward, following a decision by the bookers or a growing popularity with the public.
- Screwjob: The final result of a match deemed unfair by the public. It can be scripted or not, as in the case of the Montreal Screwjob, between Shawn Michaels and Bret Hart, where the latter lost the belt without being warned.
- Shoot: Action which breaks the kayfabe (ex: calling a wrestler by their real name). It can be scripted or not.
- Smart: Designates a wrestling enthusiast who knows the behind the scenes of wrestling or is looking to learn more.
- Spot: Action or series of actions constituting highlights of a match. Generally generates a strong public reaction. However, too many spots can damage the psychology of the match and saturate the public. Wrestlers are then pejoratively described as "spot monkeys".
- Squash: A wrestler's expeditive victory. The squash is often used to put a monster heel in the spotlight.
- Stiff: Execution of holds with excessive force. This allows the wrestler to intensify the match but with the risk of injuring their opponent.
- Turn: When a wrestler changes their alignment, going from heel to face, or vice versa. The turn generally provokes a strong public reaction.
- Tweener: A wrestler that cannot be easily classified as a face or a heel. His gimmick is often that of a rebel or an antihero who opposes authority. He can therefore break the rules while still being supported by the public.
My name is Gwen, and I am a French journalist and graphic designer, and have been a fan of wrestling since I was 10 years old.
For me, the mask is the best symbol in wrestling. It is immediately recognizable and unique for every wrestler. I started out drawing them just for fun at first, but through my research I discovered passionate lives that I wanted to share.
For this publication, we have limited ourselves to around 200 wrestlers (though more will be added) chosen according to their importance in wrestling or for their specific interests. Details were primarily derived from sources available on the Internet (Wikipedia, press articles, and fansites), and also the sites Luchawiki, Cagematch, and Wrestling database. Additional information comes from Heather Levi’s book “The World of Lucha Libre”.
Although I am a wrestling fan, I do not claim to be an expert. This subject is complicated for a journalist because reality and fiction are permanently intertwined in order to maintain the illusion (or kayfabe) of the storylines. We are always open to any suggestions or for improvement or correction.
Whether you are a fan, or maybe even a wrestler, please don’t hesitate to contact us to enrich this database. I would be particularly interested in a masked wrestler’s experiences, in order to know more about their connection to their mask. Get in touch at sup@pudding.cool.

# Svelte Starter
This [starter template](https://github.com/russellgoldenberg/svelte-starter) aims for fast and easy web development with HMR, and pre-rendered HTML for optimal static hosting.
#### Features
- [HMR](https://github.com/rixo/svelte-hmr) for lightning fast development
- Includes csv, json, and svg imports by default
- [SCSS](https://sass-lang.com/) ready (optional)
- [LayerCake](https://layercake.graphics/) preloaded for graphic development
- [Tabler-Icons](https://github.com/tabler/tabler-icons) for simple/easy svg icons
- Pre-render on deploy for a baked-out HTML with content that is hydrated on load
- Configured to make easy deploment to Github Pages
## Quickstart
```bash
npx degit russellgoldenberg/svelte-starter my-project
cd my-project
npm install
npm run dev
```
## Development
Modify content in `src` and `public/assets`.
## Deploy
```bash
npm run deploy
```
If deploying to github pages:
```bash
make github
```
## Style
CSS or SCSS both work fine. Either do within style tag or externally like:
` -->`
## Notes
Any html tags, e.g., `{@html user}` must be inside of a dom element so they can be properly hydrated.

However, the phenomenon is still alive and well in Mexico in the “Mini Estrellas” division, where the competitors face each other and wear masks inspired by famous wrestlers."},{"lang":"fr","text":"Comme les géants, les nains font partie de l’histoire et de l’imaginaire du monde forain (“carnival”). Issu du vaudeville et encore très populaire dans les années 50 aux Etats-Unis, le “midget wrestling” s’est depuis cantonné à des segments comiques. Mais, au Mexique, le phénomène est encore vivace, avec la division des “Mini Estrellas”, où s’affrontent notamment les “mascotas”, qui portent des masques inspirés de célèbres catcheurs."},{"lang":"es","text":""}]},{"wrestler":"estrella_divina","title":[{"lang":"en","text":"Exóticos"},{"lang":"fr","text":"Les Exoticos"},{"lang":"es","text":""}],"body":[{"lang":"en","text":"Lucha libre is often synonymous with machismo, or overexaggerated masculinity, but it does have space for characters, like the exótico, that challenge that stereotype. Exóticos are male wrestlers who embrace traditionally feminine traits and costumes, often performing in feather boas, headdresses, sequins or stockings. Since the 1980s, wrestlers like Rudy Reynosa, May Flowers, Pimpernela Escarlata have popularized the exótico as positive part of queer culture."},{"lang":"fr","text":"Temple de la culture “macho”, la lucha libre a utilisé, dès les années 40, la figure de l’homme efféminé, aussi appelé exotico. Comme Gorgeous Georges aux Etats-Unis, il prend un malin plaisir à provoquer les huées ou ridiculiser son adversaire. L’exotico évolue cependant à partir des années 80, grâce à Rudy Reynosa, May Flowers et Pimpernela Escarlata, qui en font une figure positive de la culture queer."},{"lang":"es","text":""}]},{"wrestler":"io_shirai","title":[{"lang":"en","text":"Luchadores"},{"lang":"fr","text":"Les Luchadoras"},{"lang":"es","text":""}],"body":[{"lang":"en","text":"Renown since the reign of Mildred Burke in 1937, women’s wrestling has had a troubled history in the United States. In Mexico, if the ring girls are still there, the luchadoras have successfully picked up the codes of lucha libre, particularly the use of the mask."},{"lang":"fr","text":"Reconnu depuis 1937, avec le règne de Mildred Burke, le catch féminin a eu un parcours houleux aux Etats-Unis. Réduit dans les années 90 à 2010 à des intermèdes sexy, il a, heureusement, été repris des forces, grâce notamment aux promotions japonaises. In response, “independent” promotions have emerged, filling different niches, such as the athletic ROH, the outrageous Chikara, and the extreme CZW."},{"lang":"fr","text":"Le catch américain s’est développé autour de multiples promotions régionales. Un “pacte de non agression” explose avec l’arrivée de Vince McMahon à la tête de la WWF (actuellement WWE), au début des années 80. En dépit de concurrences ponctuelles, la WWE domine le marché américain. Even the defunct promotion Hustle, with its unconventional stories, or Stardom, an active women’s promotion, have made their impact."},{"lang":"fr","text":"Le catch japonais est actuellement connu grâce à la New Japan Pro-Wrestling (NJPW) qui offre un très bon niveau technique, parallèlement à la promotion All Japan Pro Wrestling (AJPW). Des structures plus petites comme la NOAH, fondée par Tiger Mask II, ou la Dragon Gate, d’Ultimo Dragon, ont grandement aidé à propager le style japonais. Même la promotion défunte Hustle, aux histoires totalement décalées, et la Stardom, une promotion active de femmes, ont eu un impact."},{"lang":"es","text":""}]},{"wrestler":"blue_demon_sr","title":[{"lang":"en","text":"Mexico"},{"lang":"fr","text":"Mexique"},{"lang":"es","text":""}],"body":[{"lang":"en","text":"Mexico is the birthplace of lucha libre, and home to the oldest promotion in the world, the Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre (CMLL), founded in the 1930s. The return of wrestling to television in the 90s brought with it a new competitor in the AAA. Inspired by American wrestling (with its violence, sexualization, and more colorful gimmicks), it developed numerous partnerships with the US and Japan."},{"lang":"fr","text":"La Mexique est le berceau de la lucha libre, et abrite la plus ancienne promotion au monde, la Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre (CMLL), née dans les années 30. Avec le retour du catch à la télévision au début des années 90), la AAA apparaît comme nouveau concurrent. S’inspirant du catch américain (avec les ajouts de promo, la violence, la sexualisation et gimmick plus colorés), elle développe de nombreux partenariats avec des promotions aux Etats-Unis et au Japon."},{"lang":"es","text":""}]},{"wrestler":"super_liger","title":[{"lang":"en","text":"Canada"},{"lang":"fr","text":"Canada"},{"lang":"es","text":""}],"body":[{"lang":"en","text":"There is a famous (unattributed) saying in wrestling that goes, “in Mexico, wrestling is a religion. It is home to a number of international stars, such as Bret Hart, Chris Jericho, Chris Benoit, and more recently, Samy Zayn and Kevin Owens. Les catcheurs les plus chanceux ont des contrats, assurant des revenus et un meilleur suivi de leur santé. Mais la carrière est courte, peut être brisée à tout moment par une blessure ou amener à des décès prématurés."},{"lang":"es","text":""}]},{"wrestler":"super_amigos_super_barrio","title":[{"lang":"en","text":"Social Justice Luchadors"},{"lang":"fr","text":"Luchadors de la Justice Sociale"},{"lang":"es","text":""}],"body":[{"lang":"en","text":"Inspired by the principles of justice originating with El Santo, Super Barrio started the phenomenon of the “social luchador” in 1987, by helping those living without proper housing. He stood up for causes behind the mask, like the Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN) in Chiapas."},{"lang":"fr","text":"S’inspirant des principes de justice et d’aide aux plus humbles chers à El Santo, Super Barrio lance, en 1987, le phénomène du “social luchador”, en défendant les mals logés. Il est suivi par d’autres justiciers, que l’on peut découvrir dans le documentaire Super Amigos."},{"lang":"es","text":""}]},{"wrestler":"mil_mascaras","title":[{"lang":"en","text":"Folklore and Art"},{"lang":"fr","text":"Le Folklore et l’Art"},{"lang":"es","text":""}],"body":[{"lang":"en","text":"Even wrestling masks remain tied to their uses in culture, like African ritual masks, ancient theatre, commedia dell'arte, Noh, or carnaval.
